title.narrative: Emergency lifesaving assistance to IDPs, Refugees and communities affected by cholera and conflict in Ethiopia

description.narrative: The project focuses on addressing urgent needs to reduce avoidable mortality and morbidity among communities affected by cholera and conflict in Ethiopia. As of November 12, 2024, the country reported 57,759 cholera cases and 731 deaths (CFR = 1.27%), with weekly averages of 70–90 cases. Five of 13 regions currently have active outbreaks, with the situation worsened by conflicts and mass displacements, particularly in Amhara, Benishangul Gumuz (Kamashi zone), Oromia, and Somali (Siti zone). The country also faces a significant humanitarian crisis with approximately 4 million IDPs, 1.06 million refugees, and 2.5 million returnees as of October 2024. Access to basic social services for these populations is critically limited.The project delivers lifesaving humanitarian assistance and cholera outbreak management through targeted interventions, including emergency consultations via Mobile Health and Nutrition Teams (MHNTs), Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs), and Rapid Response Teams (RRTs). It aims to strengthen health services, disease detection, and reporting while providing essential lifesaving supplies to displaced and host communities. The project also focuses on strengthening emergency support for responders, increasing access to lifesaving care and commodities for cholera patients, enhancing cholera awareness in hotspot communities, and instituting control measures for outbreaks.A community-based approach is central to the cholera response strategy, emphasizing coordination, surveillance, case management, risk communication, and WASH. Community surveillance systems, supported by trained volunteers using simplified case definitions, will ensure prompt detection and reporting of outbreaks. Displaced populations will benefit from emergency consultations, essential medical supplies, and mentorship for community-based volunteers. Health workers will receive training and tools to address the needs of vulnerable groups, including women, children, the elderly, and persons with disabilities.Collaboration is integral to the project, involving the Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI), Regional Health Bureaus (RHBs), UN agencies (UNHCR, UNICEF, IOM), and other partners. Woreda health teams, as primary health service providers, will be engaged in planning and implementation to ensure alignment with national systems. The Regional EOCs and Woreda task forces will oversee outbreak investigations and provide technical assistance, while the Kebele RRTs will enhance community engagement.The project’s humanitarian assistance and cholera management efforts will align with Ethiopia's Public Health Emergency Management guidelines and WHO Emergency Response Framework. Coordination within the Health Cluster framework will ensure efficient response operations and better synergy among stakeholders. Contributions to WHO staff costs will enable effective technical support for six months of field operations.Key outputs include continuous availability of essential outbreak response supplies, established community-based early warning systems, effective management of outbreaks, improved access to health services for displaced populations, and enhanced complementarity in response efforts.The project is expected to benefit 26,282 individuals affected by cholera in Tigray, Amhara, Oromia, Sidama, Somali, and Afar regions, as well as 267,962 displaced persons in Amhara, Benishangul Gumuz, Somali, Tigray, and Oromia. It prioritizes lifesaving interventions and access to essential services to mitigate the impact of cholera and conflict on Ethiopia’s most vulnerable populations
